headings.title: Introduction to Primary Health Care Delivery
headings.content: Primary health care represents the first level of contact individuals, families, and communities have with the national health system. It brings health care as close as possible to where people live and work, forming an integral part of overall social and economic development. In Nigeria, this tier operates under the supervision of the Local Government Area, coordinated by the Primary Health Care Department. The core philosophy centers on universal access, equity, community participation, and intersectoral collaboration. Midwives working at this level deal with the most common health problems in the community by providing preventive, curative, and rehabilitative services. Success here directly reduces the burden on overcrowded secondary and tertiary hospitals.

headings.title: Primary Level Health Care Delivery Structures
headings.content:
The primary health care delivery system in Nigeria follows a tiered structural arrangement designed to match service capability with population distribution. This hierarchy ensures resources are used efficiently while maintaining geographical accessibility. 

- **Health Post**: The most decentralized unit, serving nomadic or remote rural settlements with basic preventive care.
- **Primary Health Clinic**: Upgraded facility serving a defined ward or village cluster with routine outpatient and basic maternity services.
- **Primary Health Centre**: A larger facility providing comprehensive maternal and child health, minor surgeries, and twenty-four-hour observation beds.
- **Comprehensive Health Centre**: The apex primary facility that often serves as a training ground and handles complex primary cases before referral.

headings.title: The Health Post: The First Point of Contact
headings.content: The health post is the lowest tier of the primary health care system, specifically designed for small, remote, or nomadic rural communities. It typically serves populations ranging from five hundred to two thousand people. Staffing usually consists of community health extension workers or trained community volunteers rather than senior professional cadres. Services focus heavily on health education, first aid, immunisation mobilization, and treatment of simple ailments like uncomplicated malaria or diarrhea. Midwives rarely run health posts independently, but they frequently supervise and conduct outreach visits to these posts from nearby primary health centres.

headings.title: Primary Health Clinics and Health Centres
headings.content: Primary health clinics and standard health centres occupy the middle tier of primary facilities, serving larger wards or village groups. Unlike health posts, these facilities provide regular outpatient clinics, routine antenatal care, normal delivery services, and basic laboratory investigations. A standard primary health centre is expected to operate twenty-four hours a day, particularly for maternity care, to prevent delayed obstetric interventions. Midwives play a central role here, conducting normal vaginal deliveries, administering oxytocics in the third stage of labor, and managing minor pregnancy complications before referral becomes urgent.

headings.title: Comprehensive Health Centres and Model PHCs
headings.content: Comprehensive health centres and model primary health care facilities represent the highest level of primary care infrastructure. They serve as referral hubs for surrounding smaller clinics and health posts within a district. These facilities feature expanded infrastructure, including modest wards for male and female admissions, a functional laboratory, an operating theatre for emergency minor procedures, and reliable utility systems. Staffing is multidisciplinary, often including medical officers, community physicians, nurse-midwives, pharmacists, and laboratory technicians. In many Nigerian states, these centres also serve as practical training sites for student nurses, midwives, and community health officers.

headings.title: Staffing and Personnel at the Primary Level
headings.content: The workforce in primary health care facilities is a diverse mix of professional, technical, and community-trained personnel. Midwives and nurses form the backbone of maternal and child health services. Community Health Officers and Community Health Extension Workers handle general outpatient consultations and community disease surveillance. Environmental health officers manage sanitation, water safety, and vector control. In smaller posts, auxiliary staff and trained traditional birth attendants or community volunteers assist with mobilization. Adequate staffing and supportive supervision remain persistent challenges in many rural Nigerian primary health facilities, directly affecting the quality of maternal care.

headings.title: Referral Systems Linking Primary Facilities to Secondary Care
headings.content: A functioning referral system ensures seamless patient movement from primary health facilities to secondary general hospitals when conditions exceed local capacity. Timely identification of obstetric emergencies—such as prolonged labor, severe pre-eclampsia, or postpartum hemorrhage—triggers the referral process. Midwives must complete a standardized referral note detailing the patient's history, findings, and emergency interventions already given. Communication with the receiving hospital and arranging reliable transport are vital components. Delays in reaching secondary care, often termed the second delay in the three delays model, contribute significantly to maternal mortality rates in Nigeria.
